problems.source_says: Study 1 of Luchini, Kaufman and Beaty (2025), 'Generative AI Does Not Erase Individual Differences in Human Creativity' (PsyArXiv osf.io/jszrn, screening candidate c475), reanalyzes this paper's data. It uses the same 263 introductory-psychology students, the same two prompts, the same GPT-3.5 interface, and the same practice task. Its reference list identifies 'Luchini et al., 2025c' as this paper (Luchini, Pronchick, Ceh, Kaufman, Johnson, Rafner and Beaty, DOI 10.31234/osf.io/xm2f5). Codebook sections 2 and 8 say that papers analyzing the same participants share a sample and get one sample_id. The c159 PDF itself names no such paper, so the form's quote is accurate, but the field is incomplete.

problems.source_says: The text says that 2 generation outliers were removed. But the correlation of the originality difference with generation prompt count reports t(254), and its partial correlation reports t(253). Both imply 256 people, so 7 were removed, not 2. Only the correlation of the diversity difference with generation count, t(259), fits 261 people. The paper is internally inconsistent here, and the form does not note it. These correlations are not coded outcomes, so neither the arm counts nor eligibility change.

confirmed: 391 students in an introductory psychology course at Pennsylvania State University were recruited for the online study (PDF p. 8, Method, Participants).

Removals: 68 for self-reported external aid, 53 for failing either of two attention checks, and 7 for scoring below 2.5 SD on an intelligence test. 391 - 68 - 53 - 7 = 263 (PDF pp. 8-9, Method, Participants).
The final sample is 263 participants (PDF p. 9), and the abstract states N = 263 (PDF p. 2).
The gender breakdown 235 + 27 + 3 sums to 265, not 263, as the form records (PDF p. 9).
The paper has one study. It is a within-subjects design: each participant wrote one AI-help story and one No-AI story, in randomized order (PDF p. 8, The Present Research; p. 9, Story Writing Task).

The counts are people, not stories: both paired t-tests have df = 262, which means 263 people, each with one story per arm, not 526 stories (originality, PDF p. 14; diversity, PDF p. 17). The form's 263 per arm fits this, and it does not double the count.

Other people-level df also fit 263: integration r has t(261) and its partial r has t(260) (PDF pp. 14-15); generation vs elaboration count has t(261) (PDF p. 16); all four Appendix D tests have t(261) (PDF p. 34).

No count by order or at assignment is reported. 391 and 263 are both odd, so the claim that 'an equal number' did each order first cannot be exact (PDF p. 9). n_randomized = null is defensible. If a number is needed, 391 is implied, because the stated removals account for every recruit.

The attention checks were in the questionnaires that followed the story task (PDF pp. 8-9). c475 p. 6 adds that the intelligence tasks also came after the story writing. So all 128 removed people were dropped after the randomized task.
The c159 PDF names no other paper using this sample (pp. 1-34 checked, references included).

No other screened Beaty-lab paper shares this sample: c158 (Lai et al. 2025) uses 208 Prolific participants (c158 md, Method), and c205 (Beaty and DiStefano 2026) uses Prolific samples (N = 234, 205, 157) and WildChat (c205 preprint, Methods).
Criterion 2 holds: 263 people were analyzed in both arms of the one randomized within-person study, which is at least 50 (PDF p. 9; df = 262 on pp. 14 and 17).
summary: The participant counts in the form are right: 391 students were recruited, 128 were removed (68 + 53 + 7), and the 263 people analyzed in both arms of the single within-person study match df = 262 in both paired t-tests, so criterion 2 holds. The coding is still refuted because the form records no sample overlap, while Study 1 of Luchini, Kaufman and Beaty (2025; candidate c475) reanalyzes the same 263 students, and because the form's 2 generation-count outliers conflict with the paper's own t(254).
